newsitem.title: UK: BRITAIN SEEKS DISCREET SPIES WITHOUT LAVISH TASTES.
newsitem.headline: BRITAIN SEEKS DISCREET SPIES WITHOUT LAVISH TASTES.

text.p: The first open advertisement for recruits to Britain's Security Service, MI5, was published on Wednesday.

Nestling among the Guardian newspaper's more usual job ads for social workers and local government officials, MI5 solicited applicants for what it called "a very special part of Her Majesty's Government -- the Security Service".
Would-be James Bonds will have to curb their appetite for fast cars and dry martinis as the salary on offer is described as "good rather than lavish".

The advertisement under the slogan "Intelligence. Use it to create waves and prevent repercussions" marks a radical change for Britain's spy services, which in the past preferred less direct approach to recruitment.
Potential agents were often identified while at university and sounded out discreetly over a glass of sherry by a tutor with connections to the secret world.
MI5, Britain's counterespionage service, began a policy of greater openness under its recently retired chief, Stella Rimington, the agency's first woman head.

With the end of the Cold War, MI5 has taken a leading role in the fight against Irish republican guerrillas. Britain's other main spy agency, the Secret Intelligence Service, MI6, handles agents abroad.
The two agencies are each estimated to have an annual budget of 125 million pounds ($200 million).
Those tempted to reply to Wednesday's advertisement were reminded that MI5 was a secret organisation and told to apply to a recruitment agency rather than MI5 itself.
"But try and avoid telling your friends about your application, because discretion is a serious part of working for the Security Service," the advertisement said.
MI5 identified marketing executives, teachers, fund raisers, overseas aid workers, academics and journalists as suitable sorts of candidates.

"Exceptional powers of communication and persuasion will make you adept at talking your way into situations with the opportunity for gathering useful information, as well as the resourcefulness to extract yourself from less promising circumstances," the ad said.

"The ability to deal with ambiguity and make decisions on partial information is essential. Security threats never conform to a neat routine and neither will your work -- so flexibility is also essential," it added.
Although describing MI5 as "a career like no other", the advertisement was coy about exactly what successful recruits would find themselves doing.

"Can you imagine a job description which said we are going to teach you to lie, cheat, tap people's phones, eavesdrop on other people's conversations, manipulate people through their weaknesses?" intelligence expert Philip Knightley told BBC television. REUTER
